Bao-2026-Intelligent technologies for tu.text: intelligent technologies for tunnel construction and maintenance: a state-of-the-art review of methods and supporting platforms xiaohua bao a , b , bowen zheng a , b , jun shen a , b , * , xiangsheng chen a , b , heqi kong a , b , junhong li a , b , xiaoqing wang c , hongzhi cui a , b a state key laboratory of intelligent geotechnics and tunnelling, college of civil and transportation engineering, shenzhen university, shenzhen, guangdong 518060, china b key laboratory of coastal urban resilient infrastructures (shenzhen university), ministry of education, shenzhen university, 518060, china c shanghai engineering and technology research center of shallow geothermal energy, shanghai 200072, china article info keywords: urban underground space shield tunnel construction and maintenance intelligent platform carbon neutralization abstract with the rapid integration of the internet of things (iot), big data, and artificial intelligence (ai), tunnel en - gineering is undergoing an accelerated shift toward intelligent construction and operation & maintenance (o & m). this paper systematically reviews the technological evolution of intelligent tunnel systems across design, construction, and operation & maintenance (o & m) phases. in the design stage, emphasis is placed on digital design tools and geological digital twins to enhance constructability. intelligent perception, real-time risk analysis, and autonomous control jointly improve construction safety and efficiency. in the o & m phase, real-time adaptive monitoring combined with predictive maintenance ensures sustained tunnel performance and resil - ience. parallelly, the development of tunnel information platforms has transitioned from standalone systems to integrated, modular, and interoperable platforms that enable multi-source data fusion, collaborative manage - ment, and real-time decision-making. this review highlights key enabling technologies, practical applications, and persistent bottlenecks, including data heterogeneity, cost-efficiency, and model generalization. looking forward, intelligent platforms are expected to evolve into closed-loop ecosystems that combine real-time sensing, ai-based optimization, and digital twin co-simulation. these systems will also embed sustainability indicators such as carbon tracking, material recycling, and lifecycle assessment to support green decision-making. collectively, the study provides a comprehensive roadmap for developing next-generation intelligent, resilient, and sustainable tunnel systems. 1. introduction with the rapid advancement of internet technologies, the internet of things (iot), and digital transformation, urban rail transit infrastructure is undergoing a new wave of intelligent upgrading. in the face of increasingly complex tunnel construction environments and rising de - mands for efficient, safe, and sustainable engineering, the intelligenti - zation of tunnel construction and o & m processes has become an inevitable trend. rather than implying that tunnels themselves are ‘intelligent ’ , this trend refers to the integration of intelligent sensing, big data analytics, and automated control technologies into lca, from design and construction to o & m. chen et al. ( chen et al., 2022 ) and zhu et al. ( song et al., 2025 ) systematically examine the applica - tion progress of deep learning in tunnels and underground engineering across seven key areas. rather than restricting attention to a single tunneling method, this review adopts a broad perspective that spans shield tunnels, drill-and-blast tunnels, mining tunnels, immersed tun - nels, and urban utility tunnels serving transportation and infrastructure needs. drawing on publications indexed in the web of science (wos) over the past five years, this paper provides a comprehensive synthesis of recent progress. this review systematically examines technological advances in intelligent tunnel engineering, focusing on sensing, data-driven modeling, automated control, real-time risk warning, and integrated platform development. by clarifying the role of intelligent technologies across the full tunnel lifecycle, covering design, construction, and o&m, it provides a holistic perspective that links technological evolution, platform integration, and sustainable development. through this lifecycle-oriented framework, the review not only assesses current progress but also highlights key challenges and outlines future di - rections. the overall technical framework is illustrated in fig. 1 . 2. key technologies for intelligent tunnel construction and o&m tunnel structures are subjected to long-te

b school of sustainability, civil & environmental engineering, university of surrey, guildford, uk abstract the digital twin (dt) technology has shown promise in transforming complex engineered systems. however, its adoption in the architecture, engineering, construction, and operation (aeco) field, particularly for built cultural heritage (bch) conservation, is still in its early stages. this study presents a systematic literature review of 85 academic publications to evaluate the current state of dt implementation in heritage building conservation and identifies areas for optimising preven - tive management. in addition, this review explores interpretations of the dt concept in this field, addressing overlaps with historical/heritage building information modelling (hbim), discusses dt functionalities and presents existing frameworks. the findings demonstrate the potential of dt to revolutionise bch conservation through a holistic approach. however, further focus is needed on features and tools for enhancing performance-based management with targeted strategies and advanced data analysis. future research should prioritise developing these aspects to fully leverage the potential of the dt paradigm in bch conservation. article history received 30 june 2023 accepted 7 september 2023 keywords built cultural heritage; data management; decision- making; digital twin; preventive conservation 1. introduction in the near future, the adaptive reuse of built heri - tage assets will be an even more fundamental driver of global and european development strategies (“the european green deal” 2019 ; “2030 digital compass: the european way for the digital decade.” 2021 ). built cultural heritage (bch) conservation is widely involved in this challenge. bch is a fundamental legacy that fosters a sense of community belonging which must be preserved. however, bch is currently facing enormous pressure due to climate change, increasing urbanisation, mass tourism, and human negligence (“joint programming initiative on cultural heritage and global change - strategic research and innovation agenda” 2020). awareness has progressively raised about the need to shift from a curative towards a preventive approach in order to keep the cultural significance and the original con - cept of heritage assets (heras et al. 2013 ; stulens, meul, and cebron lipovec 2012 ). a preventive approach suggests intervening upstream by early detection and understanding the deterioration pro - cess through regular site monitoring and mainte - nance work, reducing the need for later interventions and associated costs (jouan and hallot 2020 ; van balen 2017 ). introduced in 2002 by michael grieves (grieves 2006 , 2011 ; grieves and vickers 2016 ) in the context of product lifecycle management, the digital twin (dt) paradigm has mainly been incorporated in the aerospace domain, thanks to the contribution of nasa (eric et al. 2011 ; glaessgen and stargel 2012 ; piascik et al. 2010 ; shafto et al. 2010 ), and in the man - ufacturing industry, though gaining attention in most engineering areas. grieves and vickers ( 2016 ) describes the dt as consisting of three components, namely the real physical asset, the digital asset, and the connection between them. tao et al. ( 2019 ) add data and service, extending the three-dimensional structure of dt to five dimensions. even though the concept has been approached in different domains, it is still challenging to find a sound and unique definition of a dt (sharma et al. 2020 ). the common thread that runs throughout the different fields of application could be stated as follows: a dt is a dynamically updated asset-specific computational model(s) integrated within data-driven analyses and a decision-making feedback loops (kapteyn, pretorius, and willcox 2021 ). on the other hand, domain dependency, and poorly marked bound - aries are typically raised within the dt concept. in particular, in the civil engineering field, dt implemen - tation is at an initial stage and is limited to a few pilot contact annalaura vuoto annalauravuoto1307@gmail.com isise department of civil engineering, university of minho campus de azurém, guimarães, portugal international journal of architectural heritage 2024, vol. 18, no. 11, 1762–1795 https://doi.org/10.1080/15583058.2023.2258084 © 2023 taylor & francis projects (european commission 2021 ). some research (boje et al. 2020 ; jiang et al. 2021 ; opoku et al. 2021 ) have attempted to define the dt concept and its appli - cation in the architecture, engineering, construction and operation (aeco) domain, providing case study- based problems, and less abstraction of the topics. even more murky is the lack of definition of dts within the sub-domain of bch conservation. this work provides an extensive literature review about implementing the dt paradigm for bch preven - tive conservation to emphasise how frameworks, soft - ware, hardware, and sensor industries are interpreting the trend. to this end, a systematic literature review (slr) has been conducted. then, the paper is organised as follows. section 2 defines the research panorama on which this study focuses. the review approach is described in section 3 . section 4 collects all the literature review results and shows dt’s current usage for bch conservation. section 5 discusses the outcomes of this study, pointing out key features of the dt paradigm that are under-investigated in the bch field, and addressing conclusions and answers to the research questions introduced. 2. background research as brereton et al. ( 2007 ) suggested, a pre-review phase has been performed before starting the review process to analyse pre-existing studies and orient the formulation of the research questions (rqs) (xiao and watson 2019 ). this stage allows one to obtain a deep knowledge of the research panorama via the analysis of review papers addressing similar topics. scopus ( https://www. scopus.com ) and web of science ( https://www. webofscience.com ) databases have been questioned by using the following terms: ‘digital twin’, ‘heritage buildings’ and ‘review’ in the title, abstract and key - words. a recent slr (hou et al. 2023 ) discussed dt applications for heritage facilities management (hfm) by analysing papers published before june 2021. according to the authors, the scarcity of studies about dt application in hfm compelled a more general ana - lysis of the dt application in built environment man - agement activities. such analysis supported a prediction of future research and practice trends about dts applied to hfm. in the review, 52 key papers were selected and divided into four groups: i) construction management, ii) building o

of the online version will vary from the pagination of the print book. the design and analysis of focus group studies: a practical approach johnknodel practitioners of modern social science research are increasingly recognizing the value of focus group methodology to collect qualitative data either for its own right or to be used in conjunction with quantitative data. there is already a substantial literature on how to conduct focus groups, based largely on marketing research experience (e.g., greenbaum, 1987). far less has been written about how to design focus group studies and analyze their results, especially within the framework of social science research (but see morgan, 1988; stewart & shamdasani, 1990). this chapter provides a practical approach to design and analysis. designing a focus group study as with other approaches to studying social phenomena, designing a focus group study requires careful thought and reflection. given that focus groups can be used for a variety of purposes within social science research, the design of a focus group study will depend on its purpose. at one extreme, maximum flexibility may be desired; the number of groups to be held and even the precise characteristics of the populations to be targeted are decided in a stepwise fashion as the fieldwork progresses. such a flexible approach allows the fieldwork to stop once few new insights appear to emerge from additional sessions. this very flexible approach is probably most suitable when the research is of a very exploratory nature and when it is useful to digest the content of each successive focus group session before deciding if another is needed with any particular target group. this may be the case with pilot studies of a particular topic. likewise, if focus groups are being used to help formulate questions and response categories for a structured questionnaire, only a few sessions may be necessary; decisions on precisely how many and with whom are contingent on the utility of the sessions as they are held. at the other extreme, when qualitative information is needed on issues about which the researchers have substantial background knowledge and a reasonable grasp of the issues they wish to examine and extensive analysis of the data is anticipated, a detailed design, set in advance, is likely to be more appropriate. much of the discussion that follows relates to this latter type of design and assumes that the project will involve several subsets of the population, although many of the points are relevant even if the study concerns a single population segment. the discussion is illustrated with examples taken primarily from research on aging but could just as well have used examples from any other area of social science interest. setting objectives and formulating discussion guidelines the first step in designing a focus group study should be to define and clarify the concepts that are to be sage 1993 sage publications, ltd. all rights reserved. sage research methods page 2 of 15 the design and analysis of focus group studies: a practical approach investigated. in general, it is advisable to keep the number of broad concepts examined in a focus group moderate so that each can be examined in detail. the general concepts to be explored need to be formulated as a set of discussion guidelines that can be used by the moderator during the focus group sessions. the basic idea of the guidelines is to lay out a set of issues for the group to discuss. it is important to bear in mind that the moderator will mostly be improvising comments and questions within the framework set by the guidelines. by keeping the questions open-ended, the moderator can stimulate useful trains of thought in the participants that were not anticipated. guidelines should be kept relatively brief. remember that the objective of a focus group is an in-depth examination of the concepts being covered. if there are particular aspects of a topic that you want to ensure are probed, this can be noted in the guidelines without formulating separate questions. this way the moderator can bring them up in a more natural manner . presumably many of these points will come up spontaneously in the course of the discussion. if there are too many concepts and associated questions, there will be insufficient time to cover them before the participants become fatigued. an example of a set of guidelines intended to guide a discussion of the position and support systems of elderly in a developing country is provided in table 3.1. note that the guidelines tend to be general in nature, be open-ended, and seek to find what is going on without specifically asking directly about the situation of the individual participants. however , participants are likely to share their personal experience voluntarily to support their opinions. such personal information can also be useful, as it helps ground the discussion in reality and can serve as a concrete referent when asking about what is typical or common. note also that guidelines need not be as detailed as shown in table 3.1. if a less structured discussion is desired, a simple list of topics might even suffice, provided the moderator is well versed in the nature of the issues and thus will know when and what to probe. however, if comparisons are to be made across differently defined subgroups, relatively detailed guidelines such as those shown can help ensure that similar points are discussed across groups. sage 1993 sage publications, ltd. all rights steel-mesh roof xgboost abstract in the field of aviation, terminal building renovation and expansion projects frequently involve complex con - struction processes and the structure is in a non-static state during the construction process, resulting in sig - nificant safety risks accompanying these processes. in order to visualize and efficiently demonstrate the construction of airport terminal building renovation and expansion, and to provide a rapid decision-making analysis tool for the control of structural safety risks, a digital twin model for safety risk prediction of steel mesh frame structures is proposed. on this basis, taking the construction situation of an airport as an example, sensors were installed according to the results of the analysis of the finite element model, and a prediction model was established using the height parameters of twelve hydraulic jacks, the ambient temperature data and the stress data, in order to predict the stress changes of the key rods of the steel mesh frame. the results show that the proposed prediction model can accurately capture the stress distribution of the steel mesh frame during the overall jacking process. the stress prediction accuracy can reach 98 % for the key bars. through this method combining digital twin and machine learning, this study provides a new perspective for safety risk management in airport terminal building renovation and expansion projects, and verifies its applicability and effectiveness in actual projects through empirical studies. 1. introduction airports play a vital role in the transportation system, and as the economy develops and the demand for domestic and international movement of people and businesses grows steadily, the actual throughput of existing airports has exceeded the design capacity at that time, and they need to be modernized and expanded [ 1 ]. airport expansion projects usually include the construction of new terminals, the expansion of existing terminals and the construction of new runways and taxiways. with the increase in the number of large-span steel structure forms and the rapid expansion of the construction scale, large- span steel structure is a popular structural form for the construction of the terminal building. for the large-span steel structure, due to the huge and complex structural construction process, construction methods and construction techniques are complicated, the probability of risk in the construction phase is higher than other structures, while the construc - tion industry is increasingly demanding for safety management intelli - gence. moreover, once an accident occurs in a large and complex structure, its impact and consequences are extremely serious, causing huge property losses, casualties and serious social impacts [ 2 – 4 ]. therefore, it is crucial to predict the structural safety risks and formulate corresponding safety measures in advance to reduce the structural safety risks during the construction process and safeguard the safety of con - struction personnel and the surrounding environment. the structural safety risks of steel structures have been widely dis - cussed and investigated in a number of past studies. for example, reh - man et al. [ 5 ] used staad.prov8i to analyze and design a steel silo with the aim of determining the plate stresses, contour and critical supports, beam end force summaries, and rebar shedding in the silo structure. tian et al. [ 6 ] established a finite element model of the structure during lifting, simulated the lifting process, and analyzed the effect of the displacement difference at the lifting points, proposed a new asyn - chronous analysis method called single and staggered points, and determined the optimal limit value of the displacement difference. ruan et al. [ 7 ] proposed a construction method for sliding construction of replacement columns on large steel platforms with uneven elevations, which solved the construction challenges of steel sliding and column replacement on planes with different elevation angles. yao et al. Rashidian-2026-An IFC-based framework fo.text: full length article an ifc-based framework for semantic integration of bim and mobile crowd sensing in real-time evacuation routing mohsen rashidian * , mohammad reza malek ubiquitous & mobile gis research lab, faculty of geodesy & geomatics engineering, k. n. toosi university of technology, tehran, iran article info keywords: building information modeling (bim) mobile crowd sensing (mcs) ifc semantic interoperability indoor evacuation modeling adaptive evacuation routing digital twin abstract emergency evacuation in complex buildings benefits from tight coupling between digital building representa - tions and real-time operational data. while building information modeling (bim) provides semantically rich indoor descriptions, many evacuation systems still treat sensing technologies and bim as isolated components, resulting in static or weakly adaptive routing behavior. this paper proposes an ifc-based integration framework that establishes semantic interoperability between bim entities and mobile crowd sensing (mcs) data to enable real-time, context-aware evacuation routing. ifc models are transformed into a dynamic decision graph in which spaces, exits, and sensors are continuously annotated with live crowd-sensed information. occupant positions are estimated using wi-fi – based indoor localization supported by a two-stage crowdsensing strategy that accounts for both active and silent users. evacuation routing is formulated as a multi-criteria shortest-path problem using an extended dijkstra algorithm with dynamically updated weights reflecting distance to hazards, travel time, exit availability, and a route safety index derived from environmental conditions and crowd density. weight prior - itization is formalized using the analytic hierarchy process and examined through sensitivity analysis. the proposed framework is implemented and evaluated in a four-story academic building under three emergency scenarios. experimental results demonstrate improved evacuation effectiveness, reflected by higher in-time evacuation rates and reduced evacuation times under scenario-specific time constraints. in addition, evacua - tion times exhibit lower variability under constrained conditions, indicating stable routing behavior when egress options are limited. overall, the findings confirm that semantic coupling of bim and mobile crowd sensing enables digital-twin – like behavior for real-time emergency management and illustrates how engineering infor - matics can transform static building models into operational decision-support systems. 1. introduction real-time decision-making in safety – critical buildings increasingly relies on the integration of semantically rich digital building models with volatile, heterogeneous sensing data. from an engineering infor - matics perspective, a core challenge is achieving semantic interopera - bility between building information modeling (bim) representations and real-time sensing streams so that computational models and routing algorithms can adapt continuously to evolving indoor conditions. emergency evacuation provides a particularly demanding context: route feasibility depends jointly on building topology, hazard dynamics, and crowd behavior, and must be recomputed under strict temporal constraints. mobile crowd sensing (mcs) has emerged as a scalable paradigm for collecting occupant-level information during emergencies. by exploiting the sensing and communication capabilities of smartphones and wear - tion, visualization, and spatial reasoning [6–9] . the industry founda - tion classes (ifc) schema has emerged as an open standard for encoding bim semantics, providing object-level access to entities such as ifcspace, ifcdoor, ifcbuildingstorey, and ifcsensor. while ifc enables semantic modeling, its integration with real-time occupant-level sensing remains technically challenging due to differences in data structure, update frequency, and representation granularity. recent research has addressed aspects of bim–sensor integration from multiple perspectives. sensor-enabled bim frameworks using cctv, ble beacons, and environmental monitoring devices have been proposed, but are typically evaluated in controlled or simulation-based environments and lack full semantic alignment between ifc entities and sensing stream [10–13] . studies on ifc extensions and semantic modeling have advanced data representation and ontology design [14–18] , but often focus on static scenarios rather than operational real- time response. agent-based evacuation models and vr/ar-assisted evaluations of underground and transit environments provide insight into behavioral dynamics [19] , yet remain largely offline. bim–iot and bim–gis integration has been explored mainly within facility manage - ment contexts rather than time-critical evacuation [20–23] . recent semantic iot–bim routing models offer dynamic path plan - ning capabilities [17,18,24] , but most rely on pre-modeled conditions and do not incorporate live crowd sensing or field-level validation. overall, the literature reveals three persistent gaps. first, there is a semantic gap between ifc-based building representations and hetero - geneous crowd-sensed data streams. second, many bim-based evacua - tion systems exhibit a temporal gap, remaining static or simulation- driven without real-time adaptation. third, there is an operational gap, as empirical validations in functioning buildings remain limited. consequently, there is a need for engineering informatics methodologies that explicitly address semantic interoperability, integrate live sensing into routing logic, and demonstrate performance in operational environments. this study addresses these gaps by proposing an integrated bim–mcs framework for real-time adaptive evacuation routing. the framework resolves interoperability between ifc-based semantics and live occupant-level sensing and exploits this integration to support multi- criteria, context-aware route computation. unlike existing bim-based evacuation models that remain largely simulation-driven, and crowd - centre (operc), department of civil and building engineering, loughborough university, loughborough, leicestershire le11 3tu, uk accepted 27 february 2004 abstract the evaluation of information technology (it) is a perennial problem for businesses as they seek to improve their performance and sustain a competitive advantage. while businesses are increasing their expenditure on technology to keep abreast of competitors, organisations in the construction industry have become ‘technological laggards’. both the federal and state governments in australia have recognized the pivotal role that it can play in improving industry performance and consequently firms are being encouraged to embrace it. in obtaining performance improvements, the benefits, costs and risks of it should be identified and subsequently managed and controlled. yet, there is an absence of anchor measures that managers can confidently employ to monitor the performance of their it investments. this paper presents findings from a questionnaire survey that sought to determine the benefits, costs and risks of it investments from 126 small-to-medium sized enterprises (smes) in the australian construction industry. the questionnaire findings revealed three key findings. first, different organisation types significantly differ in the amount they invest in it but this is not influenced by firm size (i.e., in terms of turnover and number of employees). secondly, strategic benefits vary with different organisation types. third, the way in which employees adapt to change as a result of it implementation differs with firm size. based upon the reported findings a series of benchmark metrics for benefits, costs and risks of it were propagated. these metrics can serve as a reference point for initiating benchmarking, which should form an integral component of the it evaluation and learning process. d 2004 published by elsevier b.v . keywords: benchmarking; benefits; construction; costs; evaluation; it; risks; smes 1. introduction a plethora of techniques for determining the busi- ness value of information technology (it) can be found in the literature (e.g., [1 – 5]). while researchers blade digital twin (dt) abstract an improved acoustic emission (ae) based structural damage source localization method for wind turbine blade is proposed in this paper. firstly, the dispersion relations of wind turbine blade structures are achieved by a semi analytical finite element (safe) method. propagation characteristics of ae waves in key structures of wind turbine blade is then investigated in terms of the dispersion relations. based on the propagation characteristics of ae waves, including wave attenuation, wave reflection and transmission, and direction-dependent velocities, the improved structural damage source localization method is developed. furthermore, five methods are used to determine the most reasonable time difference of arrival (tdoa) for improving the numerical accuracy of damage source localization. finally, an example application of damage source localization for a “ t ” shaped structure is performed and the robustness of the developed method under gaussian white noise conditions is investigated. this work elucidates the propagation characteristics of ae waves in typical wind turbine blade structures and the contribution to structural damage source localization. the results show that the developed structural damage source localization method is efficient and reliable and it may be used as a technical basis for establishing the structural digital twin (dt) of wind turbine blades. 1. introduction with the energy transition, wind energy has become one of the most popular renewable energy sources. almost 94 gw of new installed ca - pacity of global wind turbine was added in 2021 ( gwec, 2022 ). the cost of manufacture and installation of wind turbines is expected to decline due to technology advancement. in contrast, the proportion of cost of operation and maintenance (o & m) in wind farm continues to increase ( li et al., 2021 ). the high failure rate and low-efficiency o & m strategy of wind turbines seriously squeeze the economic benefits of wind farms. recently, the proposal of the digital twin (dt) concept seems to provide a feasible solution for reducing the cost of wind energy. when applied with augmented reality, virtual reality, and mixed reality, dt can pro - vide effective, reliable and intelligent basis for decision-making ( wang et al., 2021 ). however, the research on dt application in wind turbines is still in its infancy. a key issue is that the technology of structural health monitoring for important components of wind turbines, such as the wind turbine blade (wtb), is still immature. the wind turbine blade accounts for about 20% of the total manufacture cost ( kang et al., 2021 ). because of the long-term service in the harsh natural environment, the wind turbine blade is vulnerable to various kinds of damage, such as delam - ination, debonding, and fracture. these types of damage may lead to unexpected fatigue failure or other serious accidents ( martinez-luengo et al., 2016 ). wind turbine blades are made of sandwich and composite laminates with high stiffness to weight ratio. however, they are sensitive to impact loadings ( wang et al., 2022 ) and wind turbine blades may be subjected to accidental impacts such as birds, hail, fallen maintenance tools ( celik et al., 2022 ), etc. impact damage is usually imperceptible at the early stage, but it may lead to a catastrophic failure. delamination and debonding, which are two common kinds of damages caused by impact loading, often result in a dramatic reduction in the ultimate strength of sandwich structures ( sikdar et al., 2019 ). therefore, real time structural health monitoring (shm) on structural condition is essential to provide a basis for making reasonable maintenance decisions. as an important part of dt, the shm system provides measured data, which is the basis for physical entity optimization and model updating. physical entity states of wind turbine blades can be diagnosed in real time. on the other hand, it overcomes the blindness of maintenance strategies and reduces * corresponding author. school of civil engineering, tianjin university, tianjin, 300350, china. e-mail address: turbine components. predictive maintenance schedules can be rationally developed to ensure structural safety and economy. however, current monitoring methods cannot accurately identify these types of damage at their earliest stages, which makes it difficult to establish a high-fidelity dt model for wind turbine blades. several technologies of structural health monitoring (kim et al., 2019; gomez munoz and garcia marquez, 2016; santos et al., 2016) have been used for wind turbine blades, including vibration-based damage detection, acoustic emission (ae), strain measurement, optical fiber monitoring, and ultrasonic testing technique, etc. among these technologies, ae shows the great potential to be applied to the devel - opment of dt systems for wind turbine blades. ae is a passive moni - toring tool and it is very sensitive to minor damages, such as matrix fracture, fiber fracture, debonding, delamination, etc. hence, ae is very suitable for early damage identification and damage propagation monitoring, then structural damage mode, degree and location can be characterized using advanced ae waves analysis or ae descriptors. ae has been successfully applied in civil engineering (gholizadeh et al., 2015), aerospace engineering (holford et al., 2017), and subsea pipe - lines (ho et al., 2020), etc. several experiments have been carried out to investigate the would be required in a usable and recommendable ifcowl ontology. in making this analysis, we present our implementations of an express-to-owl converter and the key features of the resulting ifcowl (rdf) semantic web 1. introduction building information modelling (bim) can be named as one of the most notable efforts in recent years regarding information management in construction industry [1]. bim environments allow to semantically describe any kind of information about the building in one 3d model, so that it can be better represented and more easily exchanged than in the case of traditional computer-aided design (cad) tools. the ifc stan- dard [2], developed by buildingsmart [3], aims at supporting these activities by providing a central “conceptual data schema and an exchange ﬁle format for bim data ” [2, scope]. in other words, using the ifc data model and ﬁle format, bim data can be exchanged between software applications, which can in turn provide extra functionality (e.g. 4d planning, 5d cost calculation, computational fluid dynamics (cfd) simulation and structural analysis). 1.1. ifc and express each ifc data model is represented as a schema in the express data speciﬁcation language de ﬁned in the 10303-11:1994 standard of the international organisation for standardisation (iso). the express language “consists of language elements which allow an unambiguous data de ﬁnition and speci ﬁcation of constraints on the data de ﬁned and by which aspects of product data can be speci ﬁed” [4]. the express lan- guage consists of the terms (e.g. types, entities, properties) and rules that must be used to build a speci ﬁc express schema (. exp). in the case of ifc, there are several available ifc express schemas, including the most well-known ifc2x3.exp, ifc2x3_tc1.exp, ifc4rc4.exp, and ifc4_add1.exp (see [5] for an overview of the speci ﬁcations). these schemas should be considered as chronologically ordered versions of one ifc schema, Zheng-2025-Prognostic digital twinning o.text: prognostic digital twinning of lattice-tubular hybrid wind turbine towers exposed to deterioration tao zheng a , junlin heng a , * , jing song b , dong zhou a , yuxiao luo a , kaoshan dai a , c a department of civil engineering, sichuan university, chengdu 610065, china b shanghai investigation, design & research institute co., ltd., shanghai 200434, china c state key laboratory of intelligent construction and healthy operation and maintenance of deep underground engineering, sichuan university, chengdu 610065, china article info keywords: machine learning high-altitude wind lattice-tubular hybrid (lth) tower digital twinning prognostic assessment abstract lattice-tubular hybrid (lth) towers, designed to harness high-altitude wind resources above 150 m, face increasing challenges of structural deterioration due to the combination of high-speed winds, large turbines, and greater tower height. these factors demand advanced methods for assessing and predictinfg structural condi - tions, particularly through prognostics. while the emerging digital twinning (dt) technology shows promising potentials for such prognostic assessment, its application to lth wind turbine towers remains unexplored. the present study develops a prognostic dt framework for deteriorating lth towers by integrating simulation models, scada, and shm data. a joint iterative approach is tailored to couple load reconstruction and model updating, while the bayesian dynamic linear model (bdlm), a probabilistic machine learning algorithm, is employed to predict future loading conditions. by leveraging virtual sensing technology, the framework enables predictive fatigue analysis of critical components, such as flanges and bolts, improving the understanding of structural reliability and integrity. a case study, based on site-specific conditions for lth applications, not only validates the framework in enhancing structural prognostics, but also inspires intelligent operation and main - tenance strategies, as well as advancements in lth tower design. 1. introduction 1.1. background and motivation according to the 2024 global wind energy council (gwec) report, global wind energy installations need to triple by 2030 to meet climate target of limiting global warming to well below 2 ◦ c, following a record 117 gw of new capacity added in 2023 [1] . this demand not only un - derscore developments in capacity installation but also necessitates the advances in wind turbine technology. recently, the lth tower [2] has been developed to install the large-scale wind turbine at escalated height, which has a promising potential to unlock the high-velocity wind resource above 150 m. unlike offshore structures, onshore lth towers emphasize modular design, lightweight construction, and factory-prefabricated components. to accommodate transportation constraints and reduce both transportation and installation costs, these towers typically employ thinner-walled main tubes reinforced by addi - tional bracing elements to maintain structural integrity. this approach facilitates standardization and efficient construction while minimizing on-site welding, thereby helping to reduce fatigue risk. however, this design also results in a significantly higher number of bolted connec - tions, which are more susceptible to fatigue-related issues [3] , resulting in a higher number of fatigue-sensitive bolted connections. however, the application of lth towers introduces structural challenges, partic - ularly around fatigue deterioration at critical connections due to higher wind loads, larger turbines, and greater tower height. especially, the bolted ring-flange of the lattice part, which connects different segments of main tubes, is highly prone to fatigue deterioration due the fracture-critical feature of high-strength bolts. uncertainty originates from the gap between idealised models and real-world conditions, making it challenging to accurately represent the true behaviour of wind turbine towers. the advanced progress in sensing technologies have led to a better understanding of the structural behaviour of wind turbines, such as the use of the supervisory control and data acquisition (scada) system for monitoring turbine operation and the structural health monitoring (shm) system for tracking structural responses [4,5] . this creates a promising opportunity for digital twin technology to provide * correspondence to: junlin heng, sichuan university, room c415, hong kong mahui building, taixin rd, shuangliu, chengdu 610211, sichuan, china. e-mail address: junlin.heng@scu.edu.cn (j. heng). contents lists available at sciencedirect structures journal homepage: www.else vier.com/loc ate/structur es https://doi.org/10.1016/j.istruc.2025.109461 received 3 march 2025; received in revised form 10 june 2025; accepted 13 june 2025 structures 79 (2025) 109461 available online 24 june 2025 2352-0124/© 2025 institution of structural engineers. published by elsevier ltd. all rights are reserved, including those for text and data mining, ai training, and similar technologies. insights in the condition of deteriorating wind turbine structures by integrating data from multiple sources and different types of physical models [6] . the original concept of digital twin comes from the aero - space industry, where it refers to the combination of a physical asset its digital counterpart, and the connection between the two [7] . beside various studies effort on the framework and possible applications of digital twins [8 – 11] , compelling demands still remains for prognostic digital twins that helps to understand the up-to-date and future struc - tural conditions of deteriorating wind turbine towers by incorporating site-specific data. this is of the first-class priority for the further pro - motion of lth towers that faces prominent concerns of the fatigue deterioration. 1.2. state-of-the-art (sota) review 1.2.1. reconstruction and prediction of loading history the reconstruction and prediction of loads is a critical scientific issue. it serves as the driving condition in digital twin simulations during the digital twin process. load reconstruction drives the dynamic oper - ation of digital twin models, while load prediction provides critical in - dicators for decision-making and maintenance of wind turbine structures. li et al. tests are conducted to verify the numerical ﬁndings. the results reveal that both the shape of the enlarged pile cap and pile strength play key roles. sensitivity analyses indicate that the eﬀ ects of cap shape and pile strength on the complex load carrying behavior of tdm piles are attributable to changes in failure mode, which depend on the mobilized skin friction and bearing of both the cap and pile body. 1. introduction soft ground improvement with deep cement mixing (dcm) piles is a soil stabilization technique that has been used to enhance the perfor- mance of on-ground and underground facilities, such as road embank- ments (e.g., [1–9]), drainage canals (e.g., [10,11]) and deep excava- tions (e.g., [12–14]). since the ﬁrst introduction of dcm piles in sweden and japan in the mid-1970s, this technique has been widely used in several countries where the soft ground layer is particularly thick [15]. the primary objectives of dcm piles include improving bearing capacity, minimizing lateral movement, reducing total and diﬀerential settlement, and increasing slope stability, as con ﬁrmed by many construction cases (e.g., [3,5,9]). past experience also suggests that using dcm piles to improve soft ground areas reduces construction time and costs. generally, dcm piles are formed with the same cross-sectional area throughout their length (hereafter called a conventional dcm pile, see fig. 1a) to transfer the applied load from the top part of the pile through the surrounding soil to the soil layer below the pile tip. under an ex- ternal load in the vertical direction, such as the foundation of a road or structure, the mobilized stress becomes largest at the pile head and then gradually decreases with depth. thus, the highest compressive stress occurs at the top part of the pile, resulting in a failure pattern that is often dominated by pile head failure if the strength of the dcm pile is insuﬃ cient. this failure pattern has been con ﬁrmed by ﬁeld test results in [16], in which more than half of tested conventional dcm piles failed due to pile head failure. when the pile head failure pattern is unfavorable, the cement content has been increased to enhance the strength of the conventional dcm pile. however, this is often an ex- pensive strategy because the deeper pile does not require high strength. moreover, many researchers (e.g., [17–19]) have revealed that the higher cement content does not economically improve the strength of cement-admixed clay. to solve the above-mentioned problem, new innovations of dcm pile techniques have been introduced, including stiﬀened and t-shaped dcm piles. a sti ﬀened dcm (sdcm) pile is a composite dcm pile consisting of a dcm socket and stiﬀ ened core to reinforce the pile at shallow depths (or pile head) as shown in fig. 1b. the t-shaped dcm (tdm) pile was ﬁrst proposed in china [20,21]. the notable feature of tdm piles is that the diameter of the pile at shallow depth (surface pile diameter) is larger than that at greater depth (pile body diameter), resulting in a cross-sectional view of the tdm pile that resembles the letter “t” (see fig. 1c). a number of studies have investigated the e ﬃ cacy of sdcm piles and their mechanical behavior, including full-scale ﬁeld tests (e.g., [7,8]), numerical analyses (e.g., [7,8,22]) and physical model tests (e.g., [22]). the studies revealed that sdcm piles can resist higher loads than conventional dcm piles of the same size. failure at the pile head under axial loading could also be mitigated. based on these studies, the understanding of the impact of a sti ﬀened core in associated with the strength of the dcm socket on ultimate pile capacity and failure be- havior has been developed and continually updated. by contrast, stu- dies on the e ﬃ cacy and key in ﬂuencing factors of the behavior of tdm piles are rather limited, probably because this innovation is still rela- tively new. based on the results from possible to reduce the size of the pile body while introducing an en- larged pile cap. moreover, it is assumed that the size of the enlarged pile cap will have an e ﬀect on the complex load transfer mechanism of the tdm pile, which, in turn, a ﬀects the bearing capacity and failure behavior. the goal of this work is to study the e ﬀect of the size of the enlarged pile cap and pile strength on the direct operations project under grant 323831. abstract as digital twins are gaining importance in various industries, research on their impact, use cases, and implementation in the field of construction is accelerating. in this study, we examine the impact of digital twins on building safety and security throughout their lifecycle, utilizing two state-of-the-art use cases for fire and anomaly detection. the solution employs advanced sensors, 3d visualizations for detecting safety and security threats, and data analysis to predict potential future threats. using the data that was collected over a seventeen-month period, we present an implementation architecture for safety and security digital twins in buildings, explore the benefits and shortcomings of such a system, and discuss the learnings applicable to different lifecycle stages of a building. this paper contributes to the creation and study of a digital twin for fire safety, analyzing its performance using two real-world use cases and reporting the implementation results. additionally, we extrapolate the learnings from the use phase of a facility to other lifecycle phases of buildings and facilities. index terms digital twin, building lifecycle management, fire safety, safety and security in buildings. i. introduction the building safety and security is a crucial topic in today’s digitalized world, requirements are essential throughout the building lifecycle. for instance, according to us fire administration, in 2020, 3500 people lost their lives to fire related accidents and there were 15200 malfunctions [8]. smart buildings are an emerging phenomenon that refers to buildings integrating and accounting for intelligence, mate- rials, construction, and control as a cohesive system with department of building, ahmadu bello university, zaria, nigeria, and richard ajayi jimoh department of building, federal university of technology minna, minna, nigeria abstract purpose – the architecture, engineering and construction (aec) industry is currently undergoing a paradigm shift as it integrates innovations such as digital twins (dt) in its activities. as a result, this study aims to ascertain the barriers affecting the implementation of digital twin (dt) technology in nigeria’s aec sector. design/methodology/approach – the study employed a quantitative approach using a questionnaire distributed via google forms, yielding 120 valid responses from built environment professionals in nigeria. the data were subjected to statistical tests such as the kolmogorov–smirnov test, cronbach’s alpha, descriptive statistics and the kruskal–wallis test. hypotheses were validated through partial least squares structural equation modelling (pls-sem). findings – the study revealed that out of the 43 identified barriers, inadequate system integration, challenges in guaranteeing interoperability, university education on the subject is deficient, and new system compatibility with legacy systems are the main barriers to implementing dt for sustainable construction practices in the aec industry of nigeria. research limitations/implications – the study was conducted in nigeria with a focus on the federal capital territory. the study identified the barriers of dt in the construction sector. practical implications – this study developed and assessed a theoretical framework, examining the relationships between variables. the findings have important implications for the construction industry, offering opportunities to improve construction processes. furthermore, the study will help improve sustainable practices within the built environment. originality/value – the study categorised the barriers of dt into the following: system integration; security- related; performance-related; organizational-related; data quality issues and environmental related issues. keywords barriers, construction 4.0, digital twin, pls-sem, sustainability, system integration paper type research paper 1. introduction the aec industry is a vital sector of the global economic development (manzoor et al., 2021). this is due to its contribution to the gross domestic product (gdp) (assaad and el-adaway, 2021). furthermore, the industry, with a market capitalisation exceeding $10tn and a global labour force of over 120 million in 2021, represents roughly chain abstract digital twin (dt) technology provides a novel, feasible, and clear implementation path for the realization of smart manufacturing and cyber-physical systems (cps). currently, dt is applied to all stages of the product lifecycle, including design, production, and service, although its application in the production stage is not yet extensive. shop-floor digital twin (sdt) is a digital mapping model of the corresponding physical shop-floor. how to build and apply sdt has always been challenging when applying dt technology in the production phase. to address the existing problems, this paper first reviews the origin and evolution of dt, including its application status in the production stage. then, an implementation framework for the construction and application of sdt is proposed. three key implementation techniques are explained in detail: the five-dimensional modeling of sdt; dt-based 3d visual and real-time monitoring of shop-floor operating status; and prediction of shop-floor op- erating status based on sdt using markov chain. a dt-based visual monitoring and prediction system (dt- vmps) for shop-floor operating status is developed, and the feasibility and effectiveness of the proposed method are demonstrated through the use of an engineering case study. finally, a summary of the contributions of the paper is given, and future research issues are discussed. 1. introduction with increasing competition in the market and changing product demands, manufacturing companies are facing the pressure of shorter product delivery times and higher product reliability. to improve production efficiency and reliability, the shop-floor manager needs to monitor the shop-floor's operating status in a timely and comprehensive manner, and predict or respond to the production exceptions as soon as possible. with the development of the internet of things, a vast amount of real-time data is collected. however, how to manage and fully use these data to display and predict the operating status of the shop-floor has always been an engineering difficulty, which is to be solved through the construction of the smart shop-floor. digital twin (dt), also known as the digital twin model (dtm), is a digital mapping model that is consistent with the corresponding phy- sical entity in the virtual space and can simulate and mirror its behavior and performance. dt technology refers to the process of using digital technology to describe the physical entities, which is the core tech- nology for the virtual-real fusion of cyber-physical systems (cps) [1,2]. the implementation process of applying dt can be divided into four steps: digital representation, synchronous mapping, simulation and prediction, and virtual and physical fusion, as shown infig. 1. first, a dt is built to accurately and digitally represent the physical entity. second, the mapping mechanism between real-time data and the dt model is established to realize the synchronous modeling between a physical entity and dt, thereby mirroring the real world based on the built dt. subsequently, through the digital models embedded in dt, including mathematical models and big data analysis models, the op- erating status of the physical entity is simulated and predicted in a virtual space. the physical entity is controlled by dt, and the data generated in physical space are continuously fed back to dt. finally, the digital models embedded in dt are iteratively optimized to achieve the co-evolution of the virtual and real worlds. hence, dt technology provides a novel, intuitive, and feasible method for solving the diffi- culties of monitoring and predicting on the shop-floor by making full use of digital space. dts, one of the specific applications of dt technology in the pro- duction stage, has been widely studied since it was proposed in 2017 by tao[3]. dts is a new paradigm for future shop-floor instances of cps in the production system. shop-floor digital twin (sdt) is a digital model in the virtual space that describes and maps all elements and processes of the corresponding physical shop-floor. it can mirror, simulate, and predict the of dts, and the construction of sdt is one of the premises in realizing dts. however, how to build and apply sdt has always been a challenge, and resolving that chal- lenge is the key to whether dt can be truly applied in the manu- facturing stage[4]and realize the monitoring and prediction of shop- floor operating status in a timely, comprehensive and intuitive manner. the remainder of this article is organized as follows.section 2in- vestigates the origin and evolution of dt and reviews the status of the application of dt in the production stage.section 3describes an im- plementation framework for the construction and application of sdt. section 4describes three key implementation techniques. insection 5, a dt-based visual monitoring and prediction system (dt-vmps) system is developed, and the proposed method is demonstrated by an en- gineering case study. section 6 summarizes the main contributions of the paper, presents the authors’ conclusions and discusses future re- search issues. 2. related work this article focuses on the modeling and use of sdt in practice for dt applications. this section first reviews the origin, evolution and connotation of dt, including its application status in the production stage, and provides a review of the state-of-the-art in the monitoring and prediction of shop-floor operating status. 2.1. origin andevolution ofdt as shown infig. 3, as dt evolves, it goes through four stages: preparation, infancy, incubation, and rapid growth and expansion. 2.1.1. preparation stage the use of the concept of “twins” in manufacturing can be traced back to nasa's apollo 13 program[5]. in this program, nasa created two identical space vehicles: one to take the astronauts into space, and the other, called the “twin,” to remain on the ground at nasa head- quarters. the purpose of the twin was to reflect the condition and predict the status of its counterpart in space through simulation, thereby helping nasa engineers and the astronauts in orbit make de- cisions in any emergency. it should be noted that the twin at this stage is a physical twin. 2.1.2. infancystage a number of key computer-aided technologies and information management systems for the manufacturing arena had already emerged by this period, including cad, cae, cam, capp, mrp, pdm, mes, and plm. in this context, grieves proposed the concept of totype stage. industry and academia are currently reconciling many competing definitions and unclear processes for developing dts. there is a compelling need to establish dts as practice in aec by developing common procedures and standards tailored to the sector ’ s procedures and use cases. this paper proposes a step-by-step workflow process for developing a dt for an existing asset in the built environment, providing a proof-of- concept case study based on the clifton suspension bridge in bristol (uk). to achieve its aim, this paper (i) reviews the state-of-the-art of dts in civil engineering, (ii) proposes a working dt-based workflow framework for the built environment applicable to existing assets, (iii) applies the framework and develops of the physical- virtual architecture to a case study of bridge management, and finally ( iv ) discusses insights from the application. the main novelty lies in the development of a versatile methodological framework that can be applied to the broad context of civil infrastructure. this paper ’ s importance resides in the knowledge challenge, value prop - osition and operation dictated by developing a dt workflow for the built environment, which ultimately rep - resents a relevant use case for the digital transformation of national infrastructure. 1. introduction advances in computational technology (e.g. digitalisation and data management) have led to a new era of revolutionary innovation, i.e. the so-called industry 4.0. the concept of a digital twin (dt) is one of the uncontested protagonists of this change: the global dt market was valued at usd $3.8bn in 2019, and it is expected to rise to usd $35.8bn by 2025 [ 1 ]. the two-thirds of large industrial companies will be deploying at least one dt in the next decade, resulting in a 10% improvement in effectiveness [ 2 ]. in the architecture, engineering and construction (aec) sector, the actual application of dts is still largely at the prototype stage, while there is a lack of established protocols and standards to develop a common narrative and guidance [ 3 ]. industry and academia are currently reconciling many competing definitions and unclear processes for developing dts, especially for existing (legacy) infrastructure which is much less likely to have a digital representation than newly-constructed ones [ 4 ]. this paper utilises the dt definition provided by the uk ’ s national digital twin programme, i.e. “ a realistic digital representation of assets, processes and systems ” with a defining characteristic of a data connec - tion between the real world and its digital representation [ 5 ]. the synchronisation between the state of the real-world asset/process/sys - tem and its virtual (also called digital or computational) representation is the key feature that distinguishes the dt from any other digital rep - resentation model (e.g. bim). the way this synchronisation is achieved, the frequency with which the virtual representation is updated and how the virtual representation is used can further characterise the dt. for example, a dt may form an active part of a cybernetic control system (like a thermostat) to directly control the behaviour of its tangible counterpart, or it may take a more passive role, e.g. informing decision- making processes in building maintenance. dts exist at many scales and levels of complexity, from a single component (e.g. bridge saddle or car acronyms: aec, architecture, engineering and construction; ai, artificial intelligence; bim, building information modelling; csb, clifton suspension bridge; csbt, clifton suspension bridge trust; dt, digital twin; fe, finite element; fem, finite element model; iot, internet of things; shm, structural health monitoring; wsn, wireless sensor network. * corresponding author. e-mail address: maria.pregnolato@bristol.ac.uk (m. pregnolato). contents lists available at sciencedirect automation in construction journal homep age: www.el sevier.com/l ocate/autcon https://doi.org/10.1016/j.autcon.2022.104421 received 19 may 2021; received in revised form 1 june 2022; accepted 6 june 2022 automation in construction 141 (2022) 104421 2 seat) or asset (e.g. bridge or train car) to systems of connected dts (e.g. a car ’ s dt sending signals to a highway dt), up to an ecosystem of con - cesses are uncertain and in their relative infancy ” [ 7 ]. the first step for establishing dts as practice in aec is to develop common frameworks and processes. current literature and practice lack practical insights into the “ real-virtual-link ” paradigm, e.g. how enquiring into the real structure should be performed and how the virtual structure should be designed and the link implemented. this paper aims to develop a step- by-step workflow process for developing a dt for an existing asset in the built environment, providing a proof-of-concept case study, based on the clifton suspension bridge in bristol (uk); the process is implemented on a specific asset which makes the concept more accessible to a range of stakeholders (industry, modellers, researchers, infrastructure man - agers), especially considering the majority of structures that do not have pre-existing bim data. the aim is achieved through the following ob - jectives : (i) reviewing the state-of-the-art of dt in civil engineering; (ii) proposing a working dt-based workflow framework for the built envi - ronment applicable to existing assets, aligned with the state-of-the-art guidance; (iii) applying the framework and developing the physical- virtual architecture for a case study of bridge management; ( iv ) discus - are critical for managing large-scale industrial facilities, yet their increasing connectivity exposes them to sophisticated cyberattacks, with a reported 44% rise in incidents by 2023. this study addresses the challenge of intrusion detection in scada systems by evaluating four advanced deep learning models, dcnv2_moe, entityembeddingmlp (ee-mlp), rtdlresnet, and temporal convolutional network (tcn), for multi-class attack classification. using a custom scadanet dataset, generated in a virtualized lab environment with nine attack scenarios (e.g., http flood, sql injection, port scan) and normal traffic, we applied comprehensive preprocessing to tackle class imbalance, high dimensionality, and temporal dependencies. the models achieved near-perfect performance, with rtdlresnet attaining a macro avg f1-score of 1.00, followed by dcnv2_moe and ee-mlp at 0.99, and tcn at 0.96. cross-dataset evaluation on an independent public scada benchmark further confirmed competitive generalization (macro avg f1-scores of 0.80–0.85), although performance naturally declined due to domain shift between laboratory-generated and real-world traffic patterns. class- specific analysis revealed robust detection of volumetric attacks but variable performance on scanning attacks, particularly tcn’s lower precision for os scans. these findings highlight the strengths of tabular and sequential architectures for scada security, offering a scalable framework for real-time intrusion detection while identifying areas for enhancing model robustness and generalizability against evolving threats. while results are derived from a virtualized laboratory environment, future semi-real-world validation in digital twin setups is planned to bridge the gap to operational scada deployments, ensuring applicability boundaries are clearly defined. to partially mitigate concerns regarding real-world applicability, the trained models were evaluated in a zero-shot manner on a publicly available sdn-based scada dataset, achieving competitive macro avg f1-scores in the 0.80–0.85 range despite domain shift. these findings highlight the strengths of tabular and sequential architectures for scada security, offering a scalable framework for real- time intrusion detection while identifying areas for enhancing model robustness and generalizability against evolving threats. scholarship council, grant/award number: 201706320312; national natural science foundation of china, grant/award numbers: 51978182, 52020105002 summary traditional post-earthquake inspection of civil infrastructure is conducted manually, taking a considerable amount of time and often putting inspectors in harm's way. this problem is exacerbated in modern cities, where millions of people can be left home- less until their residences are deemed safe to reinhabit. image collection enabled by commercial unmanned aerial vehicles (uavs) combined with computer vision-based techniques has provided an alternative with high potential for rapid post-earthquake inspection. however, the extracted images of the damage alone are inadequate to evaluate the system-level safety condition of a structure. the quality of the visual information also heavily relies on the effectiveness of the uav inspection scheme which is susceptible to environmental uncertainties. to this end, a graphics-based digital twin (gbdt) framework is developed for uav-aided post-earthquake inspec- tion of high-rise buildings and validated using a high-rise building in guangzhou, china. the gbdt is comprised of a finite element (fe) model and a photorealistic computer graphics (cg) model, with the latter being informed by the former, jointly providing as a comprehensive virtual representation of the structure so that every step of the post-earthquake inspection procedure can be planned and evaluated vir- tually. first, to avoid the cumbersome nature of constructing the graphical represen- tation of the numerous components in high-rise buildings, the cg model in the gbdt is created by automatically importing structural components from the fe model and adding nonstructural components according to the dimensions of the as-built struc- ture. this fast modeling process as well as the accuracy of the virtual presentation are validated by point cloud comparisons between the cg model and the as-built structure. subsequently, the gbdt is used to showcase the evaluation of uav flight schemes for post-earthquake inspection of high-rise buildings. to shorten flight time and place more emphasis on potential damage, fe analysis is conducted to determine the earthquake-induced damage locations. consistent damage hotspots are then received: 30 june 2023 revised: 3 february 2024 accepted: 17 april 1 | introduction earthquakes are among the most catastrophic natural disasters faced by modern societies. damage to civil infrastructure is inevitable due to the rapid urbanization in regions of high seismicity. rapid inspection and evaluation of damaged structures therefore become crucial and urgent to ensure the safety of life and property, as well as to restore normalcy to society. traditional post-earthquake inspections are usually conducted by structuralengi- neering experts based on visual checks and empirical judgment. for example, during the 1978 thessaloniki earthquake in greece, it took almost 1000 engineers about 2 months to inspect more than 150,000 apartments in 30,000 buildings within thessaloniki city and 30,000 apartments in 13,000 buildings in the surrounding rural area. this earthquake, along with the subsequent 1981 aklyonides–korinthos earthquake, led to the establishment of the earthquake planning and protection organization of greece in 1983, which marked the beginning of systematic post-earthquake inspection guidelines. 1 similarly, the u.s. applied technology council published a field manual for post-earthquake safety evaluation of buildings in 1989. 2 in 1997, china passed the law on earthquake prevention and disaster reduction 3 which provided similar guidelines. despite the standardization of post-earthquake inspection procedures by these manuals and laws, inspections are still conducted manually, and therefore are incredibly time- consuming and perilous for inspectors, especially when dealing with high-rise buildings. because of the significant heights and dimensions of such buildings, damage to the upper floors is nearly impossible to identify from the ground and thus requires extensive inspection time inside the damaged building. moreover, high-rise buildings play a major role in sheltering large populations in cities; until these buildings are inspected, the resid ents are essentially homeless. thus, means for rapid post-earthquake inspection of the civil infrastructure is direly needed. with the recent development of the drone industry, 4–7 image collection enabled by commercial unmanned aerial vehicles (uavs) provides a significant opportunity for rapid post-earthquake inspections. researchers have proposed that uav-collected images can be utilized to build com- puter graphics (cg) models with point cloud reconstruction techniques, 8,9 which can then be used for visual inspection. the capacity and effec- tiveness of the inspection can be further facilitated by automated damage detection based on the uav-collected images. early research about damage detection techniques employed heuristic feature extraction methods, applying a threshold or a classifier to the output of a manually designed filter for a particular type of damage. 10–13 to address the challenges faced by such heuristic feature extraction techniques, such as com- plex design, narrow applicability, and low accuracy, researchers have turned toward machine learning-based methods. 14,15 machine learning- based algorithms can handle several types of damage simultaneously. damage can also be projected onto a mesh model to better guide engineers in assessing structural conditions. for example, hoskere et al. 16 generated a 3d mesh model from uav-collected images of a damaged building following the 2017 central mexico earthquake. by projecting the inferred damage information onto the 3d mesh model, a condition-aware model was developed for damage documentation and higher-level inspection decisions. however, such
